name: Dispatch equipment to sites
summary: Superintendents and foremen ask the regional yard for machines and tools. The yard coordinator finds an owned unit in the yard or on another site or rents one, a mechanic checks it, a yard driver trucks it to site, and the register starts charging the project an internal rate until the unit comes back. Requests come by phone and text and are keyed into the equipment register by hand; units left idle on sites keep charging projects and keep the fleet short, and rental invoices often disagree with the dates the yard recorded.

baseline.org_archetype: A Canadian national general contractor of about 2,800 people with four regional equipment and formwork yards and an owned fleet of small and mid-size machines.
baseline.notes: Covers machines and tools other than tower and mobile cranes, which follow the crane operations process.

trigger: A superintendent or foreman asks the yard for a machine or tool for a site.
end_state: The unit has been delivered, used, returned to the yard or off-rented, and its internal or rental charges posted to the project's job cost.

volume.seasonality: Requests rise from April and peak in summer; winter adds heaters and hoarding equipment.

evidence.note: Org file estimate: about two requests per active project a month.

surge.cause: construction season (May to October), when concrete, earthworks and exterior work peak

evidence.note: As in the org file; estimate.
Time superintendents spend requesting, receiving and calling off equipment; the process map does not list superintendents.

Rental approvals; estimate.

roles.title: Yard truck driver (boom truck and flatbed)

evidence.note: The org file has 14 boom trucks but no driver role; a heavy-equipment operator with a class A or DZ licence can drive, but contractors usually employ yard drivers. Cost is the author's estimate on the org file's 1.6 loading for union trades.

systems.name: Equipment management (fleet register, rates, maintenance work orders)
Construction ERP (job cost, general ledger, payables, receivables, payroll)
AP invoice scanning and approval workflow

resources.name: Flatbed and boom trucks for yard deliveries
Regional equipment and formwork yards with repair shops

steps.name: Request equipment
steps.description: The superintendent or foreman phones, texts or emails the yard asking for a machine or tool: type and size, site, delivery day and how long it is needed. Most requests are for telehandlers, skid steers, aerial platforms, heaters, pumps and site equipment.

error.defect_description: Wrong size or attachment requested, or delivery day missing.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Log the request in the equipment system
steps.description: The yard coordinator types the request into the equipment register or dispatch board with project, cost code, requester, unit type and dates, and calls back if the request is incomplete.

error.defect_description: Request logged to the wrong project or cost code.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Check fleet availability and location
steps.description: The coordinator searches the register for an owned unit of the right type that is in the yard, coming off another site soon or out for repair, and compares the internal rate with a rental for the expected duration.

evidence.note: Sourcing split is an estimate for a contractor that owns its core fleet and rents for peaks.

steps.name: Assign and reserve the owned unit
steps.description: The coordinator assigns a specific unit number to the request in the register so no one else books it and flags it for the shop to check.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Pre-dispatch inspection and service check
steps.description: A mechanic checks the unit before it leaves: fluids, tires, hydraulics, safety devices, the operator's manual and load chart on board, and service hours against the maintenance schedule.

control.basis: Manufacturer inspection and maintenance requirements and the constructor's duty under the Occupational Health and Safety Act to keep equipment in good condition

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Repair or service the unit
steps.description: The mechanic opens a service work order, orders parts if needed and repairs or services the unit before it can go out; if repair will take too long the coordinator finds another unit.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Arrange transfer from another site
steps.description: The coordinator calls the superintendent holding the unit to agree a release date, and tells both sites when the truck will come. Superintendents often hold machines they are not using.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Get rental quotes and place the rental order
steps.description: The coordinator phones two or three rental companies for price and availability, picks one and places the rental order with delivery date, site contact and job number.

error.defect_description: Wrong rate or duration on the order.

next.condition: long-term or large rental needs approval

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Approve the rental
steps.description: The equipment and yard manager reviews long or expensive rentals, asks whether an owned unit could be freed or the rental bought out, and approves or redirects.

control.basis: Company purchasing authority limits for rentals

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Rental company delivers the unit
steps.description: The rental company trucks the unit to site on its own schedule; in the busy season popular units are booked out and delivery slips.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Book a truck or float
steps.description: The coordinator puts the move on the boom-truck schedule for the day or, for heavy machines and when the trucks are booked, hires a float carrier.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Hired float carrier moves the unit
steps.description: A float carrier picks up the unit at the yard or releasing site and delivers it to the requesting site on its own schedule.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Load and secure the unit and inspect the truck
steps.description: The yard truck driver does the daily trip inspection of the boom truck, loads the unit with the boom or ramps at the yard or releasing site, and chains and straps it to the cargo securement rules.

control.basis: Highway Traffic Act commercial vehicle daily inspection and cargo securement rules (Ontario and equivalent provincial rules)

evidence.note: Regulation named from general knowledge; text not opened.

steps.name: Drive the unit to site
steps.description: The driver drives to the project, in city traffic for most sites and up to several hours for regional jobs.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Wait for access and unload at site
steps.description: The driver waits for the site's delivery window, a clear laydown area or the gate to open, unloads the unit, gets the delivery ticket signed and drives back to the yard.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Receive and check the unit
steps.description: The superintendent or foreman checks the unit is the one asked for and undamaged, signs the delivery ticket and assigns an operator with the right training.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Record the unit on site and start internal charges
steps.description: The coordinator enters the delivery date and site against the unit in the register, which starts the internal rate charge to the project, or records the rental's on-rent date.

error.defect_description: Delivery date or site keyed wrong.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Review the site equipment list each week
steps.description: While the unit works on site, the coordinator sends each superintendent the list of units charged to the project and asks which can come back. Touch time is the total of those weekly checks for one unit; the wait is the time the unit is on site.

evidence.note: On-site durations are estimates: a week for small tools up to two months for telehandlers on a structure.

steps.name: Call the unit off site
steps.description: The superintendent tells the yard the unit is finished. Units often sit idle for days before anyone calls them off, still charging the project.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Call the rental company off-rent
steps.description: The coordinator phones the rental company to stop the rental, records the off-rent number and the pick-up date in the register.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Pick up the unit and return it to the yard
steps.description: The driver collects the unit from site when a truck is free and brings it back to the yard or straight to the next site.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Inspect the returned unit
steps.description: A mechanic checks the returned unit for damage, missing attachments, fluid leaks and service due, and records the hour meter reading in the register.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Raise a service work order and damage report
steps.description: The mechanic writes a service work order for the shop and, where the damage was caused on site, a damage report so the repair can be charged back to the project.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Close the dispatch and stop internal charges
steps.description: The coordinator records the return date in the register, which stops the internal rate charge, and marks the unit available or in the shop.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Reconcile the rental invoice
steps.description: When the rental invoice arrives the coordinator checks the rate, on-rent and off-rent dates, damage and fuel charges against the order and codes it to the project for accounts payable.

control.basis: Three-way match of rental invoices to order and off-rent record before payment

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Dispute rental charges
steps.description: The coordinator calls or emails the rental company about wrong dates, rates or damage charges and waits for a credit note before releasing the invoice.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

steps.name: Post monthly equipment charges to job cost
steps.description: At month end the equipment system calculates internal rental charges for owned units by days on site and posts them, with coded rental invoices, to each project's job cost in the ERP.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for a Canadian union general contractor that self-performs concrete.

exceptions.name: Unit needs repair before dispatch
exceptions.description: The pre-dispatch check finds a defect or overdue service; the shop repairs it or the coordinator swaps units.

exceptions.name: Wrong or damaged unit delivered
exceptions.description: The site rejects the unit because it is the wrong size or damaged and the request is sourced again.

exceptions.name: Rental billing dispute
exceptions.description: The rental invoice charges days after the off-rent call or damage the site disputes.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from request to charges posted (includes time on site)
benchmarks.population: Owned and rented units dispatched from a contractor's regional yard

evidence.note: Author's estimate: delivery in 1 to 3 days, on site two to three weeks for a typical unit, return and month-end posting within another two weeks.
Estimate.

pain_points.description: Units sit idle on sites for days before superintendents call them off, charging the project and leaving the yard short.

evidence.note: Estimate.

pain_points.description: Requests arrive by phone and text and are keyed into the register by hand; location and dates are often wrong, so internal charges and rental invoices disagree.

evidence.note: Estimate.

pain_points.description: Boom trucks are booked solid in season, so moves wait a day or go to hired floats.

evidence.note: Estimate.

assumptions: The org file has no truck driver role; the workflow adds truck-driver (not_in_org_file). Equipment operators listed in the process map operate machines on site rather than dispatch them, so they do not appear.
Time a unit spends working on site is modelled as the wait before the weekly review step; touch time there is the total of the weekly checks.
Hired float carriers and rental company deliveries are external waits with no touch time.
Superintendents and mechanics take part although the org file's process map lists only the yard coordinator, equipment manager and equipment operator.
No public source describing contractor equipment dispatch in Canada was opened; figures are tier C estimates.
